sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Mbabaram: Kager 1995 'On foot templates and root templates' (Linguistics Library 12). It is hybrid open access (cc-by-nc); the publisher PDF was downloaded, text-extracted and pp. 131-132 rendered and read as page images, logged). Sec. 4 is a secondary report of Dixon 1991 with a 332-root tabulation: heavy syllables always stressed; initial /a/ never stressed (second-syllable stress); C-initial disyllables lexically split; trisyllables mostly sigma-2, some final with initial secondary stress. It refines but does not contradict the catalog's weight-hedged coding on Dixon 1991:360, and being derivative of Dixon 1991 it does not supersede the deciding source. No paywalled or unread items remain from this search of works with stress in the title. Note from earlier check notes held by the project (not a works with stress in the title): Dixon 1991 vol. 4 is HathiTrust full view (mdp.39015021573046, seq 376 = p. 360) but page delivery is blocked from this GCP host.

new_statements.quote: Mbabaɽam stress is complex and lexically variable. Heavy syllables are always stressed (14a-b). An initial /a/ never bears main stress, which usually falls on the second syllable (14b-d). Disyllabic full-vowel roots are stressed on either the second syllable (14e-f), or the initial syllable (14 g-h). Most trisyllabic full-vowel roots are stressed on the second syllable (14i-j), some on the final syllable with an initial secondary stress (14k-l): (14) b abúu 'ground' d aráman 'woomera' e ɟibú 'no good' f miɟál 'lip' g búmba 'ashes' h láŋgil 'light' i ḏambáɽa 'nulla nulla' k gùriḏál 'eaglehawk' l gùludún 'dove'

new_statements.reading: Main stress is lexically variable and weight-conditioned: long-vowel (heavy) syllables always take it; word-initial /a/ is never stressed, so a-initial words are stressed on the second syllable; consonant-initial disyllables are split between initial and final stress with no rule; trisyllables are mostly second-syllable stressed, a minority final-stressed with initial secondary stress. Kager's root counts in (15) (152 final-stressed vs 12 initial-stressed LL roots, 93 of the 152 a-initial) quantify the pattern from Dixon's 332-root vocabulary. This is fully consistent with the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding and adds trisyllabic and secondary-stress detail the snippet chain lacks.
